title: Photothermal reverse-water-gas-shift over Au/CeO2 with high yield and selectivity in CO2 conversion
abstract: Photothermal reverse-water-gas-shift is realized with high conversion rate and selectivity of CO in the case of Au/CeO2 catalyst. Moreover, photothermal reaction rate is much higher (>10 times) than that performed under thermal condition. As indicated by the results of in-situ infrared spectroscopy and kinetic experiments, the special role of light is found to be related with the promotion of hydrogen-splitting step. The robust Au/CeO2 catalyst exhibits stable activity and CO selectivity under long-term light irradiation. It is expected that the combination of catalysts and light may afford new perspectives for the CO2 hydrogenation.
paragraphs: As a dominant energy supply, fossil fuels are widely utilized in industry field and daily life, and its ever-increasing consumption brings tremendous emission of CO2 [1]. The continuous increase of CO2 concentration in atmosphere may cause negative effect on global climate and ecosystem. To solve this problem, CO2 reutilization has become a significant issue in the worldwide research [2,3]. Among various strategies for CO2 reuse, CO2 as C1 feedstock to fabricate value-added chemicals has attracted considerable attention [[4], [5], [6]]. In this process, a crucial issue is related with the stable and inert characteristics of CO2, and additional energy is required to drive the reaction of CO2 conversion. This route may not be desirable as it further causes more CO2 emission. It is therefore of great importance to develop effective approach for CO2 conversion with a renewable energy source.

Recently emerged photothermal process seems favorable to address the sustainable demand of energy supply, since it uses solar irradiation to provide thermal energy [[7], [8], [9], [10]]. The photothermal process could enable the effective harvesting of light to drive useful reactions, such as the hydrogenation of CO2 to methane on metal/oxides (or metal/hydroxides) catalysts [7,8]. In comparison with the most work on methane by CO2 hydrogenation, little attention was paid to the photothermal reverse-water-gas-shift (RWGS) in both high conversion ratio and selectivity at low temperature. In traditional RWGS reaction, CO2 and H2 mixture passed over the catalyst and CO product was achieved through the following reaction (CO2 + H2 = CO + H2O). As an important products of CO2 conversion, CO offers high flexibility as it may be used in downstream Fischer–Tropsch for synthesizing advanced hydrocarbon products [4,5]. Consequently, it is significant to develop efficient catalysts towards photothermal hydrogenation of CO2 to CO.

Before the exploration of alternative photothermal catalysts, we should learn from the relative experiences in traditional thermal hydrogenation CO2 to CO. The popular thermal catalysts normally consist of well-dispersed metal nanoparticles supported on metal-oxides. Metal catalysts nanoparticles are responsible for the hydrogen dissociation while the oxides provide active sites for the adsorption and activation of CO2. Previous studies provided worthy information on the principles to tune the selectivity and activity of these metal/oxide catalysts towards RWGS reaction. Various metals including nonprecious metals (e.g. Cu [[11], [12], [13]] and Fe [14]) and precious metals (e.g. Pd [15], Pt [16] and Au [17]) were supported on oxides and these composite catalysts were capable of catalyzing the RWGS process. It is reported that selectivity of CO is closely related to the oxygen binding energy on metal material and weaker oxygen binding metals (e.g. Cu, Pd and Au) favored the conversion of CO2 to CO [[18], [19], [20]]. Among these metals, gold possessed relatively strong light-absorption in visible-light and could be a potential candidate for the photothermal RWGS reaction. Considering that Au particles exhibit special behaviors under light irradiation [9], photothermal process may facilitate conversion of CO2 to CO on the Au-based catalysts with optimum oxide support.

Here we constructed a robust catalyst suitable for photothermal process based on Au nanoparticles with CeO2 nanorods, which is an optimum support for CO2 adsorption and activation. In addition, a photothermal flow cell was set up for harvesting light for the CO2 hydrogenation. The as-synthesized Au/CeO2 catalyst showed much higher activity under photothermal process than that in thermal process, while almost 100% CO selectivity was achieved at the same time. And the photothermal effect on the conversion of CO2 to CO was also investigated in detail. Our results provide insight into the reaction mechanisms and key steps for CO2 hydrogenation in special photothermal process. Such understanding could be helpful to the design of efficient photothermal catalysts and widen their applications in other general heterogeneous catalysis.

All the chemicals were purchased from Aladdin Chemistry Co., Ltd. China without any further purification. CeO2 nanorods were synthesized by a hydrothermal method with reference to a previous report [1]. Briefly, a Ce(NO3)3 solution was first prepared in a 100 mL Teflon bottle by adding 0.868 g Ce(NO3)3·6H2O and 40 mL H2O. And then NaOH solution (16 g NaOH in 30 mL H2O) was added dropwise at room temperature under stirring for 30 min. Subsequently, the Teflon bottle with this mixture was put in a stainless steel autoclave, which was then sealed and heated in an electric oven at 100 °C for 24 h. After the hydrothermal reaction, white precipitates were separated by centrifugation and washed by deionized water. The CeO2 sample was further dried at 80 °C in air overnight, and then calcined at 773 K in air for one hour. The one-step synthesis of Au/CeO2 was carried out by the following photocatalytic deposition method. CeO2 sample (0.3 g) was firstly dispersed in 20 mL ethanol by ultrasonic treatment, and 0.3 mL HAuCl4 solution (58 mM) was added into the CeO2 dispersion mixture. Then the mixture was subjected to the UV treatment (360 nm, 50 W) at room temperature under vigorous stirring. After 30 min, the wine red Au/CeO2 product was collected via centrifugation and further washed by water. After dried in vacuum oven, the product was used for various characterizations and catalysis tests.

The powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were recorded on a Rigaku D/MAX-RB diffractometer with monochromatized Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.15418 nm). UV–visible diffused reflectance spectra (DRS) of the samples were obtained for the dry-pressed film samples using a UV–visible spectrophotometer (UV-2550, Shimadzu, Japan). BaSO4 was used as a reflectance standard in a UV–visible diffuse reflectance experiment. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) characterization was performed with a Philips Tecnai F30 FEG-TEM operated at 300 kV. Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP) measurement was performed to detect the composition of catalysts. The specific surface areas of samples were determined from nitrogen adsorption isotherms at 77 K (Micrometics ASAP2020) through Brunauer-Emmett-Teller equation.

The CO2 hydrogenation was performed in a homemade quartz reactor at atmospheric pressure (Fig. S1). Catalyst powder (50 mg) was spread uniformly in the cell with an interval of around 1 mm left for the gas flow. A gas mixture (1% CO2, 4% H2, balanced with nitrogen) was introduced into the flow cell at a flow rate of 3 mL min−1. In “photothermal process”, the quartz flow cell was irradiated by a visible light (Fig. S2) generated from a Xe lamp (Beijing Perfectlight Technology, PLS-SXE300) with a filter and a focusing lens, and no other assistant heating was applied. For the CO2 hydrogenation in “thermal process”, the flow cell is placed on a hotplate (IKA-HS7) to achieve the expected temperature. A thermocouple was located inside the flow cell to measure the temperature and the gaseous products were analyzed by a gas chromatography (GC-2020, Hengxin) equipped with two types of packed columns (ZKAT-Z13 PLOT, ATEO; MoleSieve 5A, Agilent) for the separation of gases (H2, CO2, CO and CH4), and two detectors (a flame ionization detector with nickel methanizer, and a thermal conductivity detector) for the quantification. The reaction rate (r) was defined as the mmole number of CO produced per total mass of catalyst per hour. Operando DRIFT spectra were collected on a FTIR spectrometer (Nicolet IS50) equipped with a MCT detector and a DRIFT accessory. The catalysts were loaded into a sample cup of reaction cell (Harrick). Before the IR measurement, the cell was flushed by Ar for 30 min at 300 °C to remove any potential contaminants. After cooling down to room temperature, the cell was irradiated by the Xe lamp or heated to a reaction temperature (623 K). Then, IR spectra (the average of accumulated 32 scans, resolution of 4 cm−1) were collected after introduction of reaction gas mixture.

A representative TEM image of as-prepared Au/CeO2 (Fig. 1) shows that the sample consists of nanorods (~ 100 nm in length) being covered by fine nanoparticles (~ 15 nm in size). HRTEM measurements were further carried out to give structural information. It can be seen that the nanorods are crystalline and have an identical lattice fringe of 0.32 nm corresponding that of CeO2 with (111) plane. Meanwhile, the nanoparticles on the nanorods should be attributed to Au metal due to the characteristic lattice fringe of 0.26 nm of Au. ICP result also gives the evidence for the existence of Au, and its content is measured to be 0.9% in atomic ratio. In addition, the surface area of CeO2 (65.7 m2 g−1) was increased to 91.3 m2 g−1 after the deposition of Au nanoparticles (Fig. S3). The XRD patterns of CeO2 in Fig. S4 shows that the location of diffraction peaks match well with the fluorite structure of CeO2 (JCPDS file no. 34–0394). No obvious XRD diffractions are observed for Au due to small content of Au particles. But for the optical properties revealed by the diffuse reflectance spectra, there is big difference between these CeO2 samples. As shown in Fig. S5a, the bare CeO2 sample only exhibits obvious absorption in the ultraviolet region (<400 nm). In comparison, the visible-light absorption is greatly enhanced on Au/CeO2 sample, and there is absorption peak at 555 nm, which is attributed to the enhanced light capture by Au nanoparticles. In addition, the band gap of the samples could be estimated from the plot of (αhv)2 versus photon energy (hv) (Fig. S5b). The value of band gap for Au/CeO2 (2.5 eV) was smaller than that for CeO2 (3.2 eV), indicating Au/CeO2 possessed good visible-light absorption.

To evaluate the catalytic performance of the Au/CeO2 sample, CO2 hydrogen was performed using a flow cell setup as illustrated in Fig. S1. In thermal process, the CO2 conversion increased with the enhancement of temperature whereas little amount (3.2%) of CO2 was hydrogenated at 400 °C (Fig. 2). The activity of catalyst was then investigated in photothermal process and the illumination power was adjusted to maintain the temperature as same as that in thermal process. At the same temperature, the CO2 conversion achieved in photothermal process was about ten times higher than that in thermal process, and reached 40% at 400 °C. Moreover, the catalysts could keep its activity well in long-term photothermal process with almost CO in nearly 100% selectivity (Fig. S6). We ever tried the CO2 hydrogenation under lower concentration of hydrogen (1% CO2 and 1% H2), and the light irradiation also exhibited similar promotion effect towards the CO2 conversion (Fig. S7). The photothermal CO2 conversion at 400 °C (12.6%) was about seven times that of thermal conversion (1.7%). However, the overall CO2 conversion at this hydrogen concentration was much lower than that at high hydrogen concentration (1% CO2 and 4% H2, Fig. 2a). This sharp contrast indicated that the reaction rate would be partly limited by the CO2 activation when the feed gas consisted of H2 and CO2 in theoretic reaction ratio. Therefore, an excessive concentration of hydrogen was utilized in this work to strengthen the activity difference of catalyst between thermal and photothermal condition.

The sharp contrast in Fig. 2a indicates that the high conversion in photothermal process should not be attributed only to the thermal effect. The Au/CeO2 catalyst may exhibit different behaviors towards CO2 hydrogenation in these two processes. To figure out which part of the catalyst (Au or CeO2) contributed to the improved activity in photothermal process, comparative experiments were also conducted over CeO2 catalyst. As illustrated by Fig. 2b, individual CeO2 exhibits almost same activity in both photothermal and thermal processes. Therefore, the contribution of CeO2 to the light-induced enhancement in CO2 conversion on Au/CeO2 could be neglected. Moreover, the CO2 conversion on CeO2 (0.8%) is much lower than that on Au/CeO2, demonstrating the decisive function of Au for the high CO2 conversion in photothermal process.

Then what is the actual reason for the special activity of Au/CeO2 in photothermal process? One possibility is that the light irradiation may change the CO2 hydrogenation mechanism, which is different from that in thermal process. If so, the apparent activation energy (Ea) in these two processes should be different. To check this hypothesis, the value of Ea for CO production was calculated from the Arrhenius plot (lnr vs. T−1), in which the rate of CO formation (r) was measured as a function of temperature. It shows that there is very little change of Ea for CO2 conversion under these two conditions (Fig. S8). This result indicates that the conversion of CO2 to CO obeyed same reaction pathways in these two processes [21].

To further explore the mechanistic details, reaction kinetics experiments were then conducted under various partial pressures. As shown in Fig. 3a, there is little change of the reaction order for CO2 molecules in these two processes, suggesting that CO2 activation is not significantly influenced by the light irradiation. In contrast, the reaction order of H2 molecules is closely related with the light irradiation (Fig. 3b). The reaction order of H2 in photothermal process is higher than that in thermal process, indicating that more hydrogen could be consumed to produce CO in photothermal process with increasing partial pressure of hydrogen. According to the classic theory of thermal catalysis, the dissociation of CO2 on metal oxide was believed to be the rate-determining step and normally occurred near the metal/metal oxide boundary. During the RWGS reaction, hydrogen was dissociated on the metal nanoparticles, moved to the interface between metal and oxide substrate, and participated into the CO2 hydrogenation [22]. Here in this work, little change of activation energy and reaction order of CO2 indicated that rate-determining step of CO2 dissociation was same in both thermal and photothermal processes. As for the H2 reaction order, the value achieved in photothermal process was bigger than that in thermal process. It was normally believed that, at the same adsorption model, lower reaction order of the reactant indicated its strong adsorption on the catalysts and potential positive effect on the reaction rate. In this work, the relationship between the H2 order and the CO2 conversion rate was not consistent with above mentioned rule. It was probably that the adsorption behavior of hydrogen in light irradiation differed a lot from that in thermal condition, which was worthy of investigation to elucidate the detailed process in future work. And at present, it was certain that light irradiation could facilitate the dissociation of H2 to enhance the rate of CO production. The reason could be that surface plasmons excited in the Au nanoparticle decayed into hot electrons, which might transfer into a Feshbach resonance of the adsorbed H2 molecule and trigger the dissociation of H2 [23,24].

Previous researchers revealed that the reaction steps for the CO production occurred through the initial CO2 and H2 dissociation, subsequent formation of CO* on the surface of catalyst, and final CO* desorption [18]. Once the H2 molecules were dissociated, the H atoms would tend to form AuH intermediates on the surface and then react with CO2 molecule. In order to analyze the difference in the dissociation of H2 under thermal or photothermal conditions, FTIR spectroscopy was further utilized to identify the intermediates during CO2 hydrogenation. When CO2 and H2 were injected into the reaction chamber, strong peaks appeared at 1590, 1473, 1310 and 1048 cm−1, which were attributed to various types of carbonates formed through the adsorption of CO2 on CeO2 substrate (Fig. 4) [25,26]. Besides these peaks, there were another two weak peaks (2118 and 1780 cm−1) emerged with the extension of reaction time under photothermal condition. The wavenumbers of these two peaks are close to that of Au-H peaks in previous reports [[27], [28], [29]]. In thermal process, similar signals of carbonate species were also observed whereas the strength of peak at 1473 cm−1 was weaker than that in photothermal process. These peaks at around 1473 cm−1 under light irradiation were not likely carbon dioxide radical anion (CO2−) formed by the CO2 activation at the reduction atmosphere. It was reported the infrared bands of CO2– located at around 1650 cm−1 and rather unstable at high temperature [30,31]. Here, the peaks at around 1473 cm−1 were attributed to the monodentate carbonate formed by the adsorption of CO2 on the CeO2 [[32], [33], [34]]. It was probable that light irradiation might promote the adsorption of CO2 on the catalyst.

In order to provide additional evidence for the assignment of the peaks at 2118 and 1780 cm−1 to Au-H, experiments were carried out in the atmosphere of pure H2. Under same photothermal condition, these two peaks were also distinguished at above-mentioned wavenumbers (Fig. S9a). In addition, it is obviously to observe a narrow hydroxyl band at 3650 cm−1, which originated from the reduction of CeO2 by the chemisorbed hydrogen. These spectral results indicate that hydrogen molecules could be dissociated on the catalyst accompanied by the formation of Au-H under photothermal condition. In contrast, the Au-H bands are almost indistinguishable in thermal process (Figs. 4 and S9b).

Based on the above experimental results, a schematic diagram was proposed to interpret the facilitated RWGS process on Au/CeO2 catalyst under photothermal condition (Fig. 5). In the hydrogenation of CO2, dissociation of H2 consumes large energy and this step plays a vital role in the reaction rate. The unique ability of Au nanoparticles in plasmon resonance enables the Au nanoparticles to absorb photo energy and generate hot electrons, which might transfer into the adsorbed H2 molecule and induce dissociation [23]. Therefore, the light irradiation is helpful to overcome energy barriers in the H2 dissociation step and favor subsequent hydrogenation of CO2 to CO.

In this work, photothermal hydrogenation of CO2 to CO was investigated over Au/CeO2 catalyst by the use of a flow cell system. The Au/CeO2 catalyst exhibited superior activity towards the RWGS reaction under light irradiation while the selectivity of CO was maintained at almost 100%. By the comparison of results from two reaction conditions, “photothermal process” and “thermal process”, the positive effect of light on the conversion of CO2 was found to be related with the hydrogen dissociation step. Operando DRIFT experiments elucidated that hydrogen molecules would be efficiently dissociated on the catalyst accompanied by the formation of AuH species under photothermal condition. As a result, the yield rate of CO was greatly improved to be about ten times higher than that under thermal process at same temperature. Present study may provide insights to the reaction mechanisms of photothermal CO2 hydrogenation and helpful guidance to the design of efficient photothermal catalysts for other heterogeneous reactions.
